extracted.intended_audience: politically engaged English citizens / readers of the Public Advertiser (Livery of London and general public)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and standards for assessing public men, choosing civic magistrates (lord mayor), and for political cooperation among friends of the people during times of constitutional crisis. Focuses on character, past conduct, fitness for extraordinary duties, and the importance of unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for shortening the duration of parliaments / triennial parliaments
rubrics_metrics.description: The shortening the duration of parliaments... triennial parliaments is the only possible resource we have left to preserve the substantial freedom of the constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocates should press warmly for triennial parliaments; public declarations of conversion to the measure are sufficient — no written formal engagement is necessary. Other measures may be argued, but triennial parliaments are presented as essential to preserve constitutional freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public support lost by soliciting office (standard of corruption)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever Mr. Wilkes shall be convicted of soliciting a pension, an embassy, or a government, he must depart from that situation, and renounce that character which... entitles him to the support of the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A public man's solicitation of offices or pensions for personal gain is a disqualifier for continued popular support; conviction of such solicitation forfeits his claim to public favour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance for sufferings and atonement when judging character
rubrics_metrics.description: How shameful is it in a man who has lived in friendship with him, to reproach him with failings too naturally connected with despair? Is no allowance to be made for banishment and ruin? Does a two years' imprisonment make no atonement for his crimes?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a person's moral and political failings, consider the mitigating effects of banishment, ruin, imprisonment, suffering and possible repentance — do not reflexively condemn without allowance for context and hardship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require proof, not abuse, when accusing corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: You brought a positive charge against me of corruption. I denied the charge, and called for your proofs. You replied with abuse... In your fortnight's letter, there is not one word upon the subject of my corruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accusations of corruption must be supported by evidence; abusive reiteration without proof is improper and undermines credibility. Demand proofs and do not accept mere invective as substitution for demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticising ministers (including wounding sovereign's feelings) can serve public good
rubrics_metrics.description: It may be highly meritorious to the public, to wound the personal feelings of the sovereign... the best of princes is not displeased with the abuse which he sees thrown upon his ostensible ministers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attacks targeted at ministers (even if they touch the sovereign's feelings) can be legitimate and beneficial when they aim to expose and correct ministerial abuse; such criticism may even stimulate the sovereign's corrective compassion toward ministers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware that degrading ministers may increase royal dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: The lower they are degraded in the public esteem, the more submissively they must depend upon his favour for protection. This... is a leading maxim in the policy of the closet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategic political critique should account for the unintended consequence that weakening public esteem of ministers can increase their dependence on royal favor and thus strengthen the crown's direct influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use honours as employment: choose candidates adapted to the work
rubrics_metrics.description: The question is not of what metal your instruments are made, but whether they are adapted to the work you have in hand... The honours of the city, in these times, are improperly, because exclusively, called a reward. You mean not merely to pay, but to employ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When conferring civic honours (e.g., lord mayor), prioritize a candidate's fitness for the extraordinary duties required at the moment rather than treating the office purely as a reward. Select people who will actively advance the public cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candidate must be willing to grant common-halls and present remonstrances
rubrics_metrics.description: Will they grant you common-halls when it shall be necessary? Will you go up with remonstrances to the King?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proper magistrate should be prepared to convene the citizenry (grant common-halls) and to present formal remonstrances to sovereign power when necessary to defend public rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candidate's firmness to confront a venal House
rubrics_metrics.description: Have they firmness enough to meet the fury of a venal house of commons?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a candidate has the resolve to stand up against a corrupt or bought legislature; the capacity to resist legislative venality is essential in times of constitutional threat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candidate's fortitude to accept imprisonment if necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Have they fortitude enough not to shrink at imprisonment?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating civic leaders, consider whether they are willing to endure personal sacrifice, including imprisonment, in defence of public liberties — fortitude under persecution is a marker of commitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candidate's willingness to hazard life and fortune for the cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Have they spirit enough to hazard their lives and fortunes in a contest, if it should be necessary?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True public defenders must be prepared to risk personal safety and property to defend the constitution; this readiness differentiates reliable champions from mere partisans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject arguments that treat extraordinary times as ordinary (rotation vs election)
rubrics_metrics.description: They insist upon a rule of rotation, which excludes all idea of election... They artfully conclude, from moderate peaceable times, to times which are not moderate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept proceduralist or complacent rules (like automatic rotation) that would nullify meaningful electoral choice in times of crisis; evaluate context and refuse to let ordinary precedents displace necessary extraordinary political judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess past conduct on public measures and elections (e.g., publishing poll)
rubrics_metrics.description: He has done every thing in his power to destroy the freedom of popular elections in the city, by publishing the poll upon a former occasion... From his past conduct, what conclusion will you draw but that he will act the same part as lord mayor?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A candidate's historical actions regarding electoral freedom and public measures are predictive; evaluate prior conduct (such as publishing polls or thwarting popular measures) as indicators of likely future behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve unity among friends of the people and prioritize common good over personal animosities
rubrics_metrics.description: Let us try whether these fatal dissensions may not yet be reconciled; or, if that be impracticable, let us guard at least against the worst effects of division... Let us employ these men in whatever departments their various abilities are best suited to, and as much to the advantage of the common cause as their different inclinations will permit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political allies should attempt reconciliation, or at minimum organize to minimize damage from factionalism; assign individuals to roles matching abilities and put the general cause above private quarrels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer public usefulness and honesty over generous but unjust bounty
rubrics_metrics.description: You will only afford one more instance, how much easier it is to be generous than just, and that men are sometimes bountiful who are not honest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to gestures of generosity that serve as substitutes for justice; evaluate actors by their honesty and justice, not mere benevolent appearances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scrutinize royal or ministerial uses of patronage and corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Corruption glitters in the van, collects and maintains a standing army of mercenaries, and at the same moment impoverishes and enslaves the country... The natural resources of the crown are no longer confided in. Corruption... introduces vice and folly triumphantly into all the departments of the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate whether crown resources and patronage are being redirected into corrupt systems of influence; such practices are destructive to national virtue and liberty and should be opposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer public men who depend on popular favour rather than access to the court
rubrics_metrics.description: To Mr. Wilkes there is no access. However he may be misled by passion or imprudence, I think he cannot be guilty of a deliberate treachery to the public. The favour of his country constitutes the shield which defends him against a thousand daggers. Desertion would disarm him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value politicians whose power is anchored in popular support rather than in personal access to court or ministerial favor, because popular dependence makes them less likely to betray the public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use severity of past misconduct proportionally and contextually
rubrics_metrics.description: The man I speak of has not a heart to feel for the frailties of his fellow-creatures. It is their virtues that afflict, it is their vices that console him... He has not been at all times proof against the extremity of distress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When condemning public figures, distinguish between habitual baseness and occasional failings attributable to extreme distress; apply moral judgments with nuance and context rather than blanket condemnation.
